title: Flex Seal Review (2026): A Good Patch, Not a Permanent Fix
description: Yes, Flex Seal is a good stopgap for small leaks; a 14 oz can covers about 12 sq ft per the maker, but it will not fix a basement wall or a pressurized pipe.
dek: Flex Seal is a good temporary patch: a 14 oz can covers about 12 sq ft per the maker, but it will not fix a basement wall, a worn roof or a pressurized pipe.
intro: Flex Seal is worth keeping on the shelf for small leaks, gutter seams and emergency patches. It is not a replacement for basement waterproofing, a roof repair or a plumber.

Flex Seal is a good temporary patch for small leaks: the maker rates a 14 oz spray can at about 12 square feet, enough for a gutter seam or a cracked flashing, not a whole wall. How well it holds depends on prep, coat thickness and sun. This review covers each product in the family, the maker's specs, owner complaints and who should skip it.
quickAnswer: Flex Seal does what a rubber coating can do: it bridges small cracks and holes on a clean, dry surface and keeps rain out of them for a while. It cannot hold back water under pressure, rebuild a rotted roof deck or stop a basement wall from wicking groundwater. Owner reviews line up with that split. They are mostly positive for gutter seams, flashing, trailer roofs and quick patches, and mostly negative from people who expected the infomercial result on a big or wet job. The standard 14 oz spray can lists at $14.99 on the maker's store.

sections.h: What Problems Does Flex Seal Fix?

blocks.p: Flex Seal fixes small, non-pressurized leaks: cracked gutter seams, gaps around vent boots and flashing, pinholes in metal trailer roofs, leaky planters, fountains, bird baths and the joint between two materials that a tube of caulk cannot bridge. The maker's own list of uses is longer, covering roofs, gutters, foundations, pools, RVs, boats and rust protection, but the common thread is the same. Every product in the family is a rubbery material that stays flexible after it cures, so it moves with the surface instead of cracking along the joint.

blocks.h3: Flex Seal spray and Flex Seal Liquid

blocks.p: The spray is the product most people mean when they say Flex Seal. It comes out as a thick liquid, settles into small cracks and dries to a satin, rubbery skin that the maker says can be painted. Flex Seal Liquid is the same idea in a can you open: a heavier, self-leveling rubber that the maker says you can brush, roll, dip or pour, and which it recommends over the spray whenever you want to brush or roll. Liquid builds a much thicker film per coat, which is why it is the better value for anything bigger than a seam. The maker advises against painting over Liquid.

blocks.h3: Flex Tape, Flex Paste and Flex Shot

blocks.p: Flex Tape is the emergency tool. The maker says it bonds to wet or dry surfaces and even under water, which makes it the one to grab for a dripping pipe while you wait for a plumber, though the maker itself calls it a temporary, emergency repair in its pool FAQ. Flex Paste fills the gaps the spray cannot: you trowel it into holes and wide seams, and it skins over in 15 to 30 minutes, per the product page. Flex Shot is a thick rubber sealant in a pressurized can that you dispense like caulk without a gun; the maker's page now says it is sold as Flex Caulk Silicone, with the same formula under a new name.

blocks.p: Flex Tape is listed for application from 20 to 120 F and rated to withstand -70 to 200 F once applied, in 4 inch by 5 foot and 4 inch by 15 foot rolls, with 8 and 12 inch widths sold separately. Flex Paste comes in cartridges, half-quart and quart jars and a MAX tub, skins over in 15 to 30 minutes and fully cures in 24 to 48 hours. Flex Shot forms a tacky skin in about 20 minutes and fully cures in 24 to 48 hours. The maker does not publish a service life, a hydrostatic pressure rating or a solids content for any of these products, and that gap is worth noting when you compare them with dedicated coatings.

sections.h: How Long Does Flex Seal Last?

blocks.p: Flex Seal has no published service life, so the honest answer is that it lasts as long as the coat stays bonded and thick enough to stay watertight, which owners report ranges from a single season to several years. The maker's page says many users report it lasting for years without cracking or peeling, and that results depend on the environment, the number of coats and maintenance. That matches the pattern in owner reviews: the long-lived repairs are thick, multi-coat patches on clean metal or masonry, and the short-lived ones are a single misted coat over dirt, rust scale or a damp surface.

Sun is the main enemy of any thin rubber film. A patch on a north-facing gutter seam, out of direct light and shed of standing water, has an easy life. A patch on a flat, south-facing shed roof sits under ultraviolet light and summer heat for hours a day, and owners commonly report that these need a fresh coat after a season or two. Ponding water speeds the decline, because a seam that stays wet for days after rain is under constant attack at its edges.

The practical way to make it last is to treat it as maintenance rather than a one-time fix. Inspect the patch each spring and fall, when you clean the gutters anyway, and add a coat where you see thinning, pinholes or lifting edges. A Flex Seal repair that you top up every year or two can keep a gutter or a trailer roof dry for a long time; one you forget about will eventually fail, usually at the edges first.

sections.h: How Much Flex Seal Do You Need?

blocks.p: Plan on one 14 oz spray can for about 12 square feet of single-coat coverage, per the maker, and plan on two or three coats for anything that has to stay watertight. In practice that means a can per 4 to 6 square feet of finished, multi-coat patch. Flex Seal Liquid goes much further: the maker rates a gallon at up to 150 square feet per coat, so a quart covering up to 37.5 square feet is usually the right size for a handful of seams.

Measure the area you will actually coat, not the size of the leak. The maker tells you to spray past the damaged area and feather the edges, and a good patch extends at least a couple of inches beyond the crack on every side. A 6 inch crack in a gutter seam therefore needs a patch closer to 10 by 6 inches, and on a gutter the coating has to wrap the bottom and both sides of the trough to keep water from running around it.

blocks.p: The last row is the reason we do not recommend Flex Seal for whole walls. At the maker's best-case 150 square feet per gallon, a single coat on a typical basement would take about seven gallons of Liquid, and a watertight film needs more than one coat. Our [basement wall sealer guide](/best-basement-wall-sealer/) shows that a masonry waterproofer such as DRYLOK Extreme does that job for a fraction of the cost and carries a pressure rating Flex Seal does not.

sections.h: Flex Seal Reviews and Complaints: What Do Owners Complain About?

blocks.p: Most Flex Seal complaints come down to five things: coats that are too thin, peeling on surfaces that were damp or dirty, the solvent smell, cans that clog, and the gap between the television demonstrations and a real roof or pipe. These are aggregated from owner reviews at the big retailers and on the maker's own pages; we have not run our own trials, so read them as patterns rather than measurements.

blocks.h3: Thin coats from the spray can

blocks.p: The most common disappointment is a spray patch that looks sealed but still leaks. Owners commonly report that one coat leaves pinholes, especially over rough or porous surfaces, and that it took three or more coats, with a day between each, to get a watertight result. The maker's instructions agree: apply several thin coats rather than one thick one, wait 24 to 48 hours between coats and keep going until no light shows through. Buyers who expected one can and one pass to fix a leak are the ones who leave the one-star reviews.

blocks.h3: Peeling on damp or dirty surfaces

blocks.p: The second pattern is peeling. Flex Seal sticks to clean, dry surfaces; it sticks badly to wet concrete, chalky paint, rust scale, gutter grime and anything with oil on it. The maker says the spray can go on a wet surface in an emergency but adheres better to a clean, dry one and should be reapplied once the area dries. Many peeling complaints come from basement walls and roofs that were never fully dry, which is exactly where moisture keeps pushing at the back of the film.

blocks.h3: Odor, sticky finish and clogged nozzles

blocks.p: Owners frequently mention a strong solvent smell, which is why the label calls for good ventilation and why we would not spray it in a closed basement or bathroom without a fan pulling air outside. Others report a finish that stays slightly tacky for days in cool, humid weather, and spray cans that clog partway through, leaving unused product. Shaking well, keeping the can warm and clearing the nozzle after each session reduces both.

blocks.h3: Not a permanent roof or plumbing fix

blocks.p: The harshest reviews come from people who used Flex Seal or Flex Tape as a permanent repair on a roof or a water line. The maker's own fine print rules much of that out: the spray withstands normal water pressure such as rain but is not made for extreme pressure, and Flex Tape's pool FAQ calls it a temporary, emergency repair. Read alongside the positive reviews, the conclusion is consistent. Flex Seal is very good at buying time and very bad at replacing a proper fix.

sections.h: Can Flex Seal Waterproof a Basement Wall?

blocks.p: Not as a whole-wall solution. Flex Seal Liquid lists stopping basement seepage among its uses, and it can seal a pipe penetration, a window well seam or the exterior face of a foundation crack. It is not formulated to soak into block or concrete the way a masonry waterproofer does, and the maker publishes no hydrostatic pressure rating for it. When groundwater pushes through a wall from the soil side, a surface rubber film on the inside tends to blister and peel away.

Start by finding out what kind of damp you have. Condensation on a cool wall is fixed with a dehumidifier and better air flow, and coating the wall does nothing for it. Seepage through the wall needs drainage outside first, then a coating made for masonry. Our guide on [how to fix a damp basement](/how-to-fix-a-damp-basement/) walks through the plastic sheet check that tells the two apart.

Where Flex Seal does help is the small stuff around the wall. A brushed coat of Liquid around a hose bib or dryer vent where it passes through the rim joist, a bead of Paste around a pipe sleeve, or a patch on the outside of a crack you have dug down to are all reasonable jobs. For the walls themselves, our [best basement wall sealer picks](/best-basement-wall-sealer/) rank coatings that are built for it, and Flex Seal Liquid appears there only as the spot-repair choice.

sections.h: Does Flex Seal Work on Roofs, Gutters and Pipes?

blocks.p: It works well on gutters, acceptably on small roof leaks as a stopgap, and poorly on pressurized pipes. Gutters are the product's best use: a leaking seam or end cap is a small, mostly non-moving joint that only sees water at normal flow, which is exactly the condition the maker describes. Scrub the seam, let it dry, and lay down two or three coats extending past the joint on each side.

Before you coat a gutter, make sure it is the seam that leaks and not water overshooting a clogged trough. Overflowing gutters stain fascia and siding in a way that looks like a leak. If debris is the real issue, [a gutter guard](/best-gutter-guards/) will do more than any sealant. Work from a stable ladder set at the right angle, with someone footing it, and never lean out past the rails to reach a seam.

On roofs, Flex Seal can stop a drip around a vent boot, a nail hole in metal roofing or a cracked flashing joint until the roof can be repaired properly. It does not replace missing or curled shingles, rotted sheathing or failed underlayment, and owners who coat a large area of worn shingles often report that the problem moves rather than goes away. The maker also notes that it is not intended for professional roofers. For a low-slope roof that needs a full coating, a purpose-made elastomeric roof coating applied at its rated thickness is the better choice.

On plumbing, use Flex Tape or Paste only to slow a drip until the pipe is replaced or a proper clamp or coupling goes on. The maker does not recommend its products for extreme pressure or for surfaces that contact drinking water, and a supply line runs at household pressure all day. Shut the water off, catch the leak and call a plumber or fit a proper repair coupling. Never use any Flex Seal product on gas lines, fuel tanks or anything carrying flammable liquids; the maker rules those out too.

sections.h: Flex Seal vs Silicone Caulk: Which Should You Use?

blocks.p: Use caulk for a joint and Flex Seal for a surface. A silicone or polyurethane caulk is made to fill a gap between two materials and stretch with it for years; it goes into the joint as a shaped bead with a defined depth, and quality sealants publish a movement rating. Flex Seal spray and Liquid coat over a surface, bridging small cracks with a film rather than filling the joint. For a window perimeter, a siding joint or a trim gap, caulk is the right tool and lasts longer.

blocks.p: For the long-term joints on a house, our [best exterior caulk guide](/best-exterior-caulk/) covers sealants made to move with siding and trim. For cracks in concrete and asphalt, a flexible crack filler poured into the gap is the better repair; our [driveway crack filler picks](/best-driveway-crack-filler/) cover the widths each one handles. Flex Seal Liquid lists concrete and asphalt repair among its uses, but a dedicated filler goes into the crack rather than over it and costs far less per foot.

sections.h: How Do You Apply Flex Seal So It Holds?

blocks.p: Clean it, dry it, then build several thin coats with a full day between them. That is the maker's method, and owner reviews suggest that almost every long-lasting repair followed it. Scrub off dirt, rust scale, loose paint and grime, wipe away oil or grease, and let the surface dry completely. Sanding or lightly etching smooth surfaces improves adhesion, per the maker's Liquid page.

For the spray, shake the can well, keep it above 60 F, and spray from 8 to 12 inches away in even, sweeping passes, covering an area wider than the leak and feathering the edges. Let each coat dry and wait 24 to 48 hours before the next. For Liquid, use it straight from the can without thinning, brush or roll it on between 32 and 120 F, and keep it out of the rain for about a day. Clean up uncured Liquid with a dry cloth and mineral spirits, not water.
SAFETY
Ventilate, protect your eyes and keep flames away

The spray is a flammable aerosol: keep it away from heat, sparks and pilot lights. Work outdoors or with windows open and a fan exhausting air. Wear gloves, eye protection and old clothes; cured rubber is hard to remove. On a ladder, keep three points of contact and do not overreach.

sections.h: Who Should Buy It, and Who Should Skip It?

blocks.p: Buy Flex Seal if you want a flexible, forgiving patch for small, non-pressurized leaks and you are willing to prep properly and apply several coats. It is a sensible thing to keep in the garage for a leaking gutter seam during a storm, a cracked downspout joint, a camper or trailer roof seam, outdoor fountains and planters, rust spots on metal, or the gap around a vent or pipe on the outside of the house. Homeowners who treat it as a stopgap or as part of yearly maintenance tend to be the satisfied reviewers.

Skip it if your problem is bigger than a patch. A basement wall that seeps needs drainage and a masonry waterproofer, a roof with worn shingles needs a roofer, a supply line under pressure needs a plumber, and anything touching drinking water, gasoline or extreme heat is outside what the maker supports. Skip the spray in particular if you dislike solvent smells and the job is indoors with poor ventilation.

If you do buy, buy the right member of the family. Pick the spray for seams and hard-to-reach spots, Liquid for anything over a few square feet, Paste for gaps and holes, Tape for a drip that needs stopping right now, and Flex Shot, now sold as Flex Caulk Silicone, for small sealing jobs around tubs and sinks. Matching the product to the job prevents most of the complaints in the reviews.

mistakes: Spraying one coat and calling it done

A single pass from the spray can usually leaves pinholes, especially on rough or porous surfaces. The maker calls for several thin coats with 24 to 48 hours between them, and for more coats until no light shows through. Budget two or three cans for a seam that has to stay watertight.
Coating a wet or dirty surface

Flex Seal bonds to clean, dry surfaces. Grime, chalky paint, rust scale and moisture are why so many patches peel. Scrub, degrease and let the area dry fully before you start; if you had to coat a wet surface in an emergency, the maker says to reapply once it is dry.
Using it to waterproof a whole basement wall

Flex Seal Liquid can seal penetrations and small spots, but it carries no hydrostatic pressure rating and costs far more per square foot than a masonry waterproofer. Water pushing from the soil side will blister a surface film. Fix drainage first, then use a coating made for masonry.
Trusting it on pressurized or drinking-water lines

The maker says its products are not made for extreme pressure and the spray is not for surfaces that contact drinking water. Flex Tape can slow a drip for a few hours, but shut off the water and get a proper coupling or a plumber. Never use it on gas lines or fuel tanks.

The spray is a flammable aerosol with a strong solvent smell. Using it in a closed basement or bathroom, especially near a gas appliance pilot light, is unsafe. Open windows, run a fan that exhausts outside, wear eye protection and keep every flame and spark source well away.
bottomLine: Flex Seal is a useful patch that its own advertising oversells. The spray, Liquid, Tape and Paste all do a real job on small, non-pressurized leaks when the surface is clean and dry and the coating is built up in several coats, and that is why so many owners keep a can in the garage. Treat it as a stopgap and a maintenance product, not a cure. For seeping basement walls, start with drainage and a masonry waterproofer from our basement wall sealer picks; for roofs and pressurized pipes, call the trade that fixes them properly.

faqs.a: Yes, for what it is designed to do. Owner reviews are mostly positive for small, non-pressurized repairs such as gutter seams, flashing gaps, trailer roofs and planters, provided the surface was clean and dry and several coats went on. Reviews turn negative when people expect it to fix a failing roof, a seeping basement wall or a pressurized pipe permanently.

faqs.q: What are the most common Flex Seal complaints?
faqs.a: Owners most often complain that a single spray coat still leaks, that patches peel off damp or dirty surfaces, that the solvent smell is strong, that cans clog before they are empty, and that it failed as a permanent roof or plumbing repair. Most of these trace back to prep, coat thickness or using it beyond what the maker supports.

faqs.q: Can you use Flex Seal on a basement wall?
faqs.a: On small spots, yes. Flex Seal Liquid can seal around pipe penetrations, window well seams and the outside of a foundation crack. As a whole-wall waterproofer it is a poor choice: it has no published pressure rating, water from the soil side tends to push it off, and a masonry waterproofer covers the same wall for far less money.

faqs.q: Can you paint over Flex Seal?
faqs.a: It depends on the product. The maker says the spray can be painted any color once it is dry. For Flex Seal Liquid, the maker advises against painting over it. Flex Tape mostly will not take paint, though the maker suggests a coat of the spray as a primer if you want to try.

faqs.q: Is Flex Seal safe for drinking water?
faqs.a: No. The maker says the spray is not for surfaces that contact drinking water, and Flex Tape has not been checked for drinking-water contact. Flex Seal Liquid's page says it is safe for rain barrels once fully cured but does not address potable water. Do not use any of them on water tanks, wells or supply pipes that carry drinking water.

faqs.q: Are UAL Flex sealant reviews about Flex Seal?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. We found no product sold under the exact name UAL Flex, and several unrelated sealants use Flex in their names, including automotive seam sealers and construction silicones. Check the maker on the label before reading reviews. Flex Seal itself is sold by the Flex Seal Family of Products through flexsealproducts.com and major retailers.

faqs.q: How long does Flex Seal take to dry?
faqs.a: Per the maker, the spray is dry to the touch in about 2 to 3 hours and fully cured in 24 to 48 hours. Flex Seal Liquid is dry to the touch in 6 to 12 hours and cures in 24 to 48 hours. Wait 24 to 48 hours between coats for both, and longer in cool or humid weather.
